questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'grid formula chart' in this lesson?
options: To provide a quick-reference summary of the square/rectangle counting formulas for different grid sizes, rather than re-deriving them each time
To replace the need to understand the formulas
To only list formulas for triangles
To show only worked examples, no formulas
questions.rationale: A grid formula chart consolidates the square and rectangle counting formulas into a single quick-reference summary, saving time re-deriving them each time.

questions.question: What does 'counting by direction' help ensure when counting triangles in a grid?
options: That only the largest triangle is counted
That triangles are counted in alphabetical order
That triangles pointing in every valid orientation (not just the most obvious one) are all counted
That only right-angled triangles are included
questions.rationale: Counting by direction ensures triangles in every valid pointing orientation — not just the most visually obvious one — are included in the total.

questions.question: What is the 'rotation rule' likely used for in figure counting?
options: Physically rotating the paper the figure is drawn on
Checking whether a candidate figure remains valid when considered from a different orientation, to catch figures easy to miss from only one viewing angle
Only applies to circular figures
Rotating the final numeric answer
questions.rationale: The rotation rule involves checking a candidate figure from different orientations, which helps catch valid figures that are easy to overlook when only considering one fixed viewing angle.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'congruent' and 'the same figure' when counting?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Congruent figures always overlap completely
Congruent figures should never be counted at all
Congruent figures are equal in shape and size but are still separate, distinct figures if located in different positions; only truly identical position and boundary makes them 'the same figure'
questions.rationale: Congruent figures share the same shape and size but occupy different positions, so each is counted separately — only an identical position and boundary makes two figures 'the same' one.

questions.question: What is a 'nested figure'?
options: A smaller figure that lies completely inside a larger figure, sharing part or all of its boundary
A figure with no boundary
A figure made entirely of dashed lines
A figure that changes size over time
questions.rationale: A nested figure sits entirely within a larger figure, often sharing part or all of its boundary with the outer shape.

questions.question: What does 'shared vertices' refer to when counting figures?
options: Vertices that are never valid
Only one figure may ever touch a given vertex
Multiple valid figures can meet at or share a common corner point without being the same figure
Vertices shared between figures should be ignored
questions.rationale: Several distinct valid figures can legitimately meet at a shared corner point without that making them the same figure — this needs to be handled correctly during counting.

questions.question: What does 'shared edges' refer to?
options: Edges that cannot be part of any figure
Multiple valid figures can share a common boundary line segment without being the same figure
Only squares can share edges
Shared edges automatically merge two figures into one
questions.rationale: Just like shared vertices, multiple distinct figures can share a common edge as part of their boundary without becoming the same figure.

questions.question: What is the 'missing-line trap'?
options: Drawing an extra unnecessary line
Confusing a line with a curve
Forgetting to label a vertex
Mistakenly counting a figure whose complete boundary isn't actually present in the original diagram
questions.rationale: This trap involves counting a figure that looks complete but is actually missing part of its true boundary in the original diagram.

questions.question: What is the 'crossing-line trap'?
options: Two lines that never actually cross
Mistakenly treating two lines that merely cross as if they formed a shared vertex or boundary, when they don't define a valid figure there
A trap that only applies to circles
Confusing a crossing point with the figure's center
questions.rationale: This trap occurs when two lines simply crossing (intersecting) is mistaken for them forming a valid shared boundary or vertex for a new figure, when it isn't.

questions.question: Why does an intersection between two lines potentially 'create new triangles'?
options: Intersections never create new figures
The intersection point can serve as a new vertex, allowing smaller triangles to form using it as a corner, which weren't present before the lines crossed
Intersections only ever create new squares
Intersections destroy any triangles already present
questions.rationale: A new intersection point can act as a vertex for smaller triangles that use it as a corner, meaning crossing lines can genuinely add new valid triangles to the count.
